example:
The evidence of `requirements.cli.check` read `parse`. The requirement is
re-authored but not yet committed, and the new record does not read `parse`.
The committed versions in the window still name it, so
`habeas status --coverage` does not warn. If the new record had read `parse`,
its contents on disk would cover it even before the commit.
{test}`requirements.references.coverage.history`
rationale:
**Verdict:** the tests adequately check the example `requirements.references.coverage.uncommitted`.

**The example is concrete.** It describes one case. `rules.check` is re-authored but not committed, and its new record no longer reads `parse`. Earlier committed versions in the window still name `parse`, so `habeas status --coverage` does not warn about it. It also states a counterfactual: a new record that did read `parse` would cover it from its on-disk contents, even before the commit.

**Main test.** `tests/coverage.rs#fn[uncommitted_records_count_as_they_are_on_disk]` carries a {test} reference to the example. It uses the fixture `project()`, whose `src/lib.rs` has `parse`, `render` and `helper`. Its helpers are `record` (which writes `evidence/<name>.json` with the outline inputs read), `commit` and `warned` (which lists the function names warned about).
- `record(rules.check, [parse])` then `commit`: `warned` is `[render, helper]`. `parse` is covered by the committed record.
- `record(rules.check, [])` with no commit: `warned` is still `[render, helper]`. This is the example's main assertion. The re-authored record on disk no longer reads `parse`, yet `parse` is not warned because the committed history still names it.
- `record(rules.render, [render])` with no commit: `warned` becomes `[helper]`. This checks that uncommitted on-disk contents count as coverage before any commit. An implementation that read only committed history would fail here.

**Shallow-clone test.** `tests/coverage.rs#fn[an_uncommitted_record_does_not_make_a_full_shallow_history_incomplete]` also carries a {test} reference to the example. It checks that an uncommitted new record that reads `helper` is counted on disk, with `incomplete` still false and `warned` equal to `[parse]`. This supports the same behavior in a shallow clone.

**Limit of the tests.** The counterfactual in the example is checked with a new uncommitted record that reads `render`, not with a re-authored record that reads `parse`. The mechanism is the same, because on-disk contents cover the item before any commit. The tests would only miss an implementation that treated modified records differently from new ones. The example does not name that edge case, so I do not count it as a gap.
